subject: economics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Two goods with a positive cross elasticity of demand (XED) are:
questions.explain: A positive XED means a rise in one good's price raises demand for the other, indicating substitutes.

questions.q: The statutory incidence of an indirect tax falls on the producer, but the burden passed to consumers is greatest when demand is:
questions.explain: When demand is inelastic consumers keep buying, so firms can pass on most of the tax through higher prices.

questions.q: A 'nudge' in behavioural economics is a policy that:
options: Imposes a large tax to change behaviour
Alters the choice architecture to influence behaviour without removing options
questions.explain: Nudges change the way choices are presented to steer behaviour while preserving freedom of choice.

questions.q: Making automatic pension enrolment the default option exploits which behavioural insight?
questions.explain: Default options exploit inertia, as people tend to stick with the pre-set choice rather than opt out.

questions.q: A point inside (below) the production possibility frontier indicates:
options: Productively efficient use of all resources
Inefficient use of resources or unemployment
questions.explain: Points inside the PPF show resources are unemployed or used inefficiently, so output could rise with no opportunity cost.

questions.q: Demand is said to be perfectly inelastic when the PED equals:
questions.explain: Perfectly inelastic demand has a PED of zero, shown by a vertical demand curve where quantity does not respond to price.

questions.q: Which statement is a normative economic statement?
options: Unemployment fell by 50,000 over the year
A 1% rise in price reduced quantity demanded by 2%
The government ought to raise the minimum wage
questions.explain: Normative statements involve value judgements about what ought to be, rather than testable facts.

questions.q: 'Anchoring' as a behavioural bias means that consumers:
options: Rely too heavily on an initial reference value when making decisions
questions.explain: Anchoring describes over-reliance on a first piece of information, such as an original price, when judging value.

questions.q: A necessity good with few substitutes typically has demand that is:
questions.explain: Necessities with few substitutes have inelastic demand because consumers continue buying despite price changes.

questions.q: An increase in the price of a substitute good will, ceteris paribus:
options: Cause a movement along the demand curve
Shift the demand curve for the original good rightwards
Shift the demand curve for the original good leftwards
questions.explain: A dearer substitute makes the original good relatively cheaper, raising its demand and shifting the curve right.

questions.q: In behavioural economics, 'bounded rationality' refers to the idea that:
options: Decision-making is limited by information, time and cognitive capacity
questions.explain: Bounded rationality recognises that limited information and mental capacity prevent fully rational optimisation.

questions.q: Producer surplus is the area:
options: Below the demand curve and above price
Below the supply curve and below price
Above the supply curve and below the market price
questions.explain: Producer surplus is the difference between the price received and the minimum price firms would accept, shown above the supply curve.

questions.q: If a firm raises price and total revenue rises, demand for the product must be:
questions.explain: When demand is inelastic, the proportionate fall in quantity is smaller than the price rise, so revenue increases.

questions.q: A negative cross elasticity of demand (XED) between two goods indicates they are:
questions.explain: Complements have negative XED because a rise in one good's price reduces demand for the jointly consumed good.

questions.q: The price elasticity of demand (PED) is calculated as:
options: % change in quantity demanded / % change in income
Change in quantity / change in price
% change in price / % change in quantity demanded
% change in quantity demanded / % change in price
questions.explain: PED measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a price change, so quantity is divided by price.

questions.q: A subsidy granted to producers will, ceteris paribus:
options: Shift the supply curve to the left and raise price
Shift the supply curve to the right and lower equilibrium price
Shift the demand curve to the right
questions.explain: A subsidy lowers production costs, shifting supply right, increasing quantity and lowering market price.

questions.q: Opportunity cost is best defined as:
options: The total cost of all alternatives forgone
The money price paid for a good
The next best alternative forgone when a choice is made
The sunk cost of a previous decision
questions.explain: Opportunity cost is the value of the single next best alternative sacrificed, not the sum of all alternatives.

questions.q: A good with a PED of -0.4 is described as:
questions.explain: A coefficient between 0 and -1 means demand is price inelastic, so quantity changes proportionately less than price.

questions.q: Scarcity arises fundamentally because:
options: Wants are unlimited but resources are finite
questions.explain: The basic economic problem is that finite resources cannot satisfy unlimited human wants.

questions.q: A specific (per-unit) indirect tax shifts the supply curve:
options: Vertically upwards by a constant amount
Vertically upwards by a larger amount at higher prices
questions.explain: A specific tax adds a fixed amount per unit, shifting supply up by the same vertical distance at every quantity.

questions.q: An outward shift of the entire PPF is most likely caused by:
options: A reallocation of resources between the two goods
An increase in the quantity or quality of factors of production
A movement from inside to a point on the curve
questions.explain: Economic growth shifting the PPF outward requires more or better resources or improved technology.

questions.q: A normal good that is a luxury has a YED that is:
questions.explain: Luxuries are income elastic with YED greater than one, so demand rises more than proportionately with income.

questions.q: Price elasticity of supply (PES) tends to be more elastic when:
options: The time period considered is very short
Stocks of finished goods are high and capacity is spare
questions.explain: Spare capacity and available stocks let firms expand output quickly in response to price, raising PES.

questions.q: A PPF that is concave (bowed outwards) to the origin reflects:
options: Constant opportunity cost between the two goods
Decreasing opportunity cost as output rises
Increasing opportunity cost as more of one good is produced
questions.explain: A concave PPF arises because resources are not equally suited to both goods, so opportunity cost rises as output shifts.

questions.q: In the price mechanism, the rationing function refers to:
options: Prices rising to allocate scarce goods to those willing to pay
Prices incentivising producers to supply more
Prices signalling where resources should move
questions.explain: The rationing function uses rising prices to distribute scarce goods to consumers who value them most.

questions.q: Consumer surplus is best described as:
options: The difference between the price paid and the maximum consumers were willing to pay
The deadweight loss from a tax
The amount firms receive above marginal cost
The total revenue earned by firms
questions.explain: Consumer surplus is the gap between the maximum a consumer would pay and the price actually paid.

questions.q: An increase in consumer income, with the good being normal, will:
questions.explain: For a normal good, higher income raises demand at every price, shifting the demand curve rightwards.

questions.q: At the midpoint of a straight-line, downward-sloping demand curve, PED is:
questions.explain: Along a straight-line demand curve, the midpoint has unit elasticity where total revenue is maximised.

questions.q: Income elasticity of demand (YED) for an inferior good is:
questions.explain: An inferior good has a negative YED because demand falls as consumer income rises.

questions.q: The signalling function of prices means that prices:
options: Are set by the government to ration goods
Always remain stable in free markets
Convey information about where resources should be allocated
questions.explain: Price changes signal to producers and consumers where resources are scarce or abundant, guiding allocation.
